explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is a Ruby library (a gem) named Money for representing, manipulating, formatting, and converting monetary values. It is not a full-stack web app but a domain library with clear internal modules and extension points.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   Top-level directories and files:  
   • lib/money – source code, subdivided into:  
     – bank (exchange logic: Base, SingleCurrency, VariableExchange)  
     – currency (currency metadata, loader, heuristics)  
     – locale_backend (formatting backends: I18n, legacy)  
     – money (core Money class: arithmetic, allocation, constructors, formatting)  
     – rates_store (in-memory store)  
     – version.rb  
   • config – JSON currency definitions (ISO, backward compatibility, non-ISO)  
   • sig – RBS signatures mirroring lib structure (for static typing)  
   • spec – RSpec tests covering every module  
   • Gemfile, Rakefile, README, CI workflows, LICENSE, etc.

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - Describes core features: Money and Currency classes, integer-cents storage, exchange via banks & stores, formatting backends, extensibility for custom banks or stores.
   - No high-level diagram provided.

4. How to draw the system design diagram  
   a. Main components (boxes):  
      1. Money API (lib/money/money)  
      2. Currency subsystem (lib/money/currency + config JSON)  
      3. Exchange Bank subsystem (lib/money/bank/*)  
      4. Rate Store subsystem (lib/money/rates_store/*)  
      5. Locale Backend subsystem (lib/money/locale_backend/*)  
      6. External Integrations (I18n gem, custom ActiveRecord or Redis stores)  
   b. Relationships & data flows (arrows):  
      • Caller → Money API (instantiate, compare, arithmetic, format, exchange)  
      • Money API → Currency subsystem (lookup iso_code, subunit, symbol, exponent; read JSON via loader)  
      • Money API → Locale Backend (format rules; I18n calls)  
      • Money API → Exchange Bank → Rate Store (get/add rates; VariableExchange delegates to RatesStore)  
      • Rate Store → persistent store implementations (Memory, ActiveRecord, Redis, or custom)  
   c. Architectural patterns & design principles:  
      - Modular Ruby code organized by responsibility  
      - Strategy pattern for Bank (Base vs SingleCurrency vs VariableExchange)  
      - Adapter pattern for Rate Store implementations  
      - Separation of concerns: currency metadata, exchange logic, formatting  
      - Dependency injection: default_bank, locale_backend, custom stores  
   d. Key technologies & libraries:  
      - Ruby language & RBS signatures (sig/)  
      - JSON config files  
      - I18n gem (optional formatting)  
      - RSpec for tests  
      - Rails ActiveRecord or Redis for custom stores  

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram to this library project  
   - Focus on the core gem boundaries: show how lib/money is partitioned into sub-modules.  
   - Emphasize extension points: Bank and Rate Store abstractions where users plug in custom implementations.  
   - Show how configuration (JSON) is loaded into Currency subsystem.  
   - Highlight the formatting backend switch (legacy vs I18n).  

6. Diagram elements to include  
   - Clear boxes labeled for each module/subsystem  
   - Directional arrows showing “calls,” “delegates to,” or “loads from”  
   - Color coding or shapes:  
     • Core modules (Money API, Currency) in one color  
     • Exchange path (Bank → Rate Store → external store) in another  
     • Formatting path (Locale Backend → I18n or legacy) in a third  
   - Notes on arrows indicating method names (e.g., Money#exchange_to calls Bank#exchange, Bank#get_rate)  

7. Emphasis on detail  
   - Capture every major class cluster as a component.  
   - Show JSON config files feeding the Currency loader.  
   - Illustrate default components (Memory store) and how to replace with custom ones.  
   - Make it easy for a new developer to see where to hook in custom behavior.  

By following this breakdown, your system design diagram will accurately reflect Money’s modular architecture, show its core responsibilities, and highlight its extension points.  
</explanation>
